abstract: This NBER working paper analyzes firm-level data on AI adoption, investment, and workforce effects using a novel survey of approximately 6,000 senior executives across US, UK, German, and Australian firms. The study finds that 69% of firms actively use AI, with higher penetration among younger and more productive organizations. Over two-thirds of business leaders regularly employ AI, though average engagement is only 1.5 hours per week. Despite high adoption rates, leadership reports minimal backward-looking effects: approximately 90% of firms report no employment or productivity changes from AI over the past three years. However, executives anticipate substantial medium-term effects, projecting 1.4% productivity gains, 0.8% output growth, and 0.7% employment reduction within three years. A notable expectations gap emerges between employers (who project workforce reductions) and employees (who forecast 0.5% employment growth).
keyFindings: 69% of surveyed firms actively use AI, with adoption concentrated in younger and more productive organizations, suggesting a digital divide that may widen over time.
Despite high adoption rates, approximately 90% of firms report no employment or productivity changes from AI over the past three years, indicating a gap between adoption and measurable impact.
Executives project significant near-term effects: 1.4% productivity gains, 0.8% output growth, and 0.7% employment reduction within three years — a marked contrast with reported past effects.
Average executive AI engagement is only 1.5 hours per week despite two-thirds of leaders using AI regularly, suggesting shallow integration into core workflows.

A notable expectations gap exists between employers (projecting 0.7% workforce reduction) and employees (forecasting 0.5% employment growth), raising questions about whose expectations will prove more accurate.
methodology: Cross-national survey of approximately 6,000 senior business executives across the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia. The survey collects both retrospective assessments of AI's effects over the preceding three years and forward-looking projections for the next three years. Novel survey design combines firm-level adoption data with executive and employee expectations about AI's workforce impacts.
qualifiers: Survey data reflects executive perceptions and expectations rather than measured outcomes. The retrospective finding of minimal effects may reflect genuine small impacts, difficulty of attribution, or executive inattention to gradual changes. Forward-looking projections are inherently uncertain and may reflect either informed judgment or media-influenced expectations. Self-reported adoption rates may be inflated by broad definitions of AI. Cross-national comparisons are complicated by different labor market institutions and AI policy environments.
